title: Neodustria Phase 21 Closed-Loop Autonomous Scientific Discovery Campaign

parsed_json.scientific_hypothesis: Linear Euler-Bernoulli predicts deflection scales as Fy/h^3; at large deflections geometric stiffening will cause sublinear force-deflection and deviation strongest for thinnest beam at highest load

Linear Euler-Bernoulli predicts stroke proportional to F/h^3; 49.55mm at thin/high-load suggests large-deflection geometric stiffening, so test same high load at max thickness to isolate h-scaling and check cubic law breakdown

At low force linear bending dominates stroke ~ F/h^3, while at 10N large deflection causes membrane stiffening; testing thin beam at minimum force will establish linear baseline to quantify stiffening ratio.
Stroke scales ~F/(h^3) in linear regime but saturates due to geometric stiffening at large deflection; testing opposite corner isolates thickness vs load effects

Thin beams (h~0.7mm) are already in membrane-dominated geometric stiffening at 0.5N (22mm stroke, only 2.2x increase for 20x load), while thick beams (h~1.7mm) remain bending-dominated (15.5x increase). Stroke transitions from linear F/h^3 to sublinear F^(1/3) scaling; center point will locate transition.

Linear beam theory predicts stroke proportional to F/h^3, but large transverse deflection induces membrane tension causing geometric stiffening to stroke proportional to (F/h)^(1/3); mid-thickness at max load tests transition from bending-dominated to membrane-dominated regime

Linear bending predicts stroke ~ F/h^3, but large deflections cause membrane stiffening toward ~F^(1/3); thick beam transition onset is unconstrained, so probe mid-load thick case to locate break from linearity

At low load deflection follows linear Euler-Bernoulli scaling ~F/h^3, but thin beams under higher loads exhibit geometric stiffening (membrane stretching) causing sub-linear F-stroke response; testing thin beam at intermediate load maps transition.
